# Glass HQ material renderer

MIT-licensed subset of Glass HQ at upstream `9f5bfc7daa7be5d20a41b94d841b8f065de655fc` with the WebGL2 port from Guangcai's `a24ffb03`. The local import uses a TypeScript GLSL string for Next.js and defines the small pixel-buffer type locally so the WebGPU renderer stays out of the dependency graph. The independently licensed `@lisse/core` v0.7.2 path distribution in `../lisse-core/` provides the continuous-corner outline. The application renders the optical source in DOM and uses the generated displacement and rim planes with SVG filters.

The reading controls also use the source implementations of `attachGeometryMotion`, `attachInteraction` and `attachNativeControlMotion` from the same Guangcai checkout. The font menu uses the Glass-HQ detach path and its traced union waypoints. The site adapter prepares WebGL2 maps for those waypoints and blends adjacent maps in its bounded DOM compositor. The slider uses the original control motion with a native range and a local copy of the live rail. Imports between TypeScript files omit the emitted extension for Next.js and resolve Lisse through the local ESM distribution.

The PNG encoder feeds raw rows to the same deflate stream directly on this site. This avoids a temporary Blob URL in WebKit during route navigation.

The material resource adapter in `site/lib/glass-material-cache.ts` now preserves each waypoint's requested DPR (resting surfaces use display DPR capped at 2), retains decoded images, pins maps actually used by the current frame, and bounds concurrent generation, LRU entries, decoded/reserved bytes and encoded-string storage. Speculative prewarming is lower priority than visible demand; disposal does not dispose the caller-owned renderer.

`dom/map-encoder.ts` and `dom/map-encoder.worker.ts` are adapted from the MIT-licensed Guangcai `a24ffb032381218b36a01ec306917b6069d573c3` versions of those same paths. The Vite inline-worker import is replaced by a Next-compatible `new Worker(new URL(..., import.meta.url), { type: "module" })`. A worker failure keeps the original pixel buffer available for fallback. The fallback is serialized and uses the same lossless PNG representation, with cooperative batches for row filtering, CRC and base64 instead of placing an entire map batch on the main thread. Shader code, material fields, rims and license text are unchanged. Worker bundling, image decoding and actual frame latency still require browser/device validation; resource diagnostics are not a claim of successful final compositor pixels.


Next/Turbopack treated the TypeScript worker URL as a raw copied asset during integration. The shipped URL therefore points to the self-contained `dom/map-encoder.worker.js`, generated from the reviewed TS entry and the same PNG encoder by `node site/vendor/glass-hq/scripts/bundle-material-worker.mjs` (uses the workspace's existing esbuild). The generated file has no runtime imports or TypeScript syntax; a worker-thread test executes this exact artifact and compares its PNG output. Rebuild it whenever its TS entry or encoding dependencies change.

Default decoded accounting is 16 MiB steady plus at most 16 MiB of demand-only transition headroom. Speculative prewarming cannot borrow that reserve. Frame pin replacement trims unused old-theme/morph resources back to the steady budget. The encoded-string budget has its own bounded transition reserve. Only an individually oversized decoded map steps down its requested raster ratio toward 1x; the cache key records that effective ratio. A resource still too large at 1x, or an individual encoded resource that cannot fit its steady limit, reports an explicit resource error rather than remaining pending forever. These bounds cover decoded/encoded cache resources and admitted raw-map estimates; GPU framebuffer/atlas scratch remains owned and accounted by the renderer.


Resting morph endpoints resolve their DPR against the current display request even when an already-open morph plan retains an older endpoint DPR. Intermediate waypoints continue to honor their explicit motion DPR. This avoids retaining low-resolution resting maps after a same-size move between displays.


CI and local validation can check the committed worker without writing it:

```sh
node site/vendor/glass-hq/scripts/bundle-material-worker.mjs --check
```

This bundles the current TypeScript dependency graph in memory and compares the complete generated bytes, including worker queue/error logic, with the shipped JS. Missing or stale output exits nonzero. The existing `site/tests/glass-material-encoder.test.ts` invokes this check as part of `npm test` and verifies that check mode does not change the artifact or its modification time. Run the same command without `--check` to regenerate intentionally.

## Cold geometry and staged resources

The reading adapter now runs the existing morphology/union arithmetic in a
separate geometry Worker; see [geometry worker details](scripts/README-morph-worker.md).
Relative layout coordinates are normalized to a 1/64 CSS-pixel grid before
planning and keying, while live placement remains continuous. This prevents
sub-layout floating-point noise from generating another full path on release.
The original fixed geometry fixture remains byte-identical.

Material GPU, PNG encoding and Image.decode work has separate bounded queues
and current/next/background priority. Raw buffers are budgeted alongside the
existing decoded/encoded budgets; only demanded work may borrow transition
headroom. Traces use per-request IDs and absolute monotonic timestamps. Worker
elapsed slices and Promise waits are wall-clock durations, not CPU ownership.
Cold diagnostic mode disables predictive prewarming; it does not claim that
browser network caches or the GPU process were reset.
